title: Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning - CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning - Risk Management
subject: CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning

questions.q: During an Invitation for Bids (IFB) for a construction project, vendors are required to submit a Bid Bond representing 5% of their total bid price. What is the primary purpose of this Bid Bond?
options: To cover any physical damage the contractor causes during construction.
To ensure that if awarded, the vendor will actually sign the contract at their bid price and provide the required performance and payment bonds.
To pay the wages of the contractor's employees if the company goes bankrupt.
To guarantee that the project will be finished ahead of schedule.
questions.explain: A Bid Bond protects the agency if the lowest responsive and responsible bidder refuses or is unable to sign the contract or provide required final bonds. If they back out, the surety compensates the agency (typically for the difference between the low bid and the next lowest bid).
questions.subject: CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning

questions.q: Which type of surety bond guarantees to the public agency that the contractor will complete the project in accordance with the specifications, terms, and conditions of the contract?
questions.explain: A Performance Bond guarantees the faithful performance of the contract. If the contractor defaults or abandons the project, the surety company steps in to ensure the project is completed, either by hiring another contractor or paying the penal sum of the bond.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning

questions.q: The Miller Act (and state-level 'Little Miller Acts') require a specific bond on public construction projects to protect subcontractors and material suppliers. Why is this bond uniquely necessary in public procurement?
options: Because subcontractors do not sign contracts.
Because unpaid subcontractors cannot legally place a mechanic's lien on public government property; the bond provides an alternative avenue for them to seek payment.
Because public agencies usually refuse to pay general contractors.
Because it ensures the public agency gets a prompt payment discount.
questions.explain: In private construction, an unpaid subcontractor can place a lien on the building. Since public property cannot be seized by a lien, the Payment Bond serves in place of a lien, guaranteeing that subcontractors and suppliers will be paid if the general contractor defaults on their obligations.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning

questions.q: A surety bond is a three-party agreement involving the Principal, the Surety, and the Obligee. In a public works contract, who is the Obligee?
questions.explain: In a surety bond, the Principal is the contractor performing the work. The Surety is the financial institution guaranteeing the work. The Obligee is the entity that is protected and receives the benefit of the bond—which is the public agency.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning

questions.q: What is the fundamental difference between Insurance and a Surety Bond in risk management?
options: Insurance is a two-party agreement where losses are expected and pooled; a Bond is a three-party guarantee of performance where the surety expects no losses and seeks repayment from the contractor if a claim is paid.
Insurance guarantees a project's completion, whereas a bond only covers medical injuries.
There is no difference; the terms are synonymous in contract law.
Bonds are required by law for all IT procurements, while insurance is only for construction.
questions.explain: Insurance protects the insured against fortuitous (accidental) risks and assumes losses will happen across a pool. A Surety Bond is an extension of credit; the surety guarantees performance to a third party (the agency) and demands indemnification (repayment) from the principal (contractor) if a claim is triggered.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning

questions.q: To protect the agency from third-party lawsuits if a vendor's delivery driver accidentally damages a citizen's car while backing into the agency loading dock, the vendor must be required to carry:
options: Commercial General Liability (CGL) and Automobile Liability Insurance.
questions.explain: Commercial General Liability (CGL) covers third-party bodily injury and property damage resulting from the vendor's operations. Automobile Liability specifically covers damages caused by the vendor's vehicles during the course of business.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning

questions.q: When hiring an architectural firm to design a new bridge, a public buyer must require Professional Liability Insurance, also commonly known as:
questions.explain: Professional Liability or Errors & Omissions (E&O) Insurance protects the agency if a professional consultant (like an architect, engineer, lawyer, or IT designer) makes a negligent mistake, error, or omission in their professional advice or design that causes financial harm.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning

questions.q: If a roofing contractor's employee falls and is severely injured while repairing a public building's roof, which insurance policy is designed to cover the injured employee's medical costs and lost wages?
questions.explain: Workers' Compensation is a statutory insurance requirement that provides medical benefits and wage replacement to employees who are injured during the course of employment.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning

questions.q: During the pre-solicitation phase of a ground-up facility construction project, the risk manager insists the contract require a policy to protect against fire, wind, or vandalism damage to the partially completed structure and materials stored on site. What policy covers this?
questions.explain: Builder's Risk insurance is a specialized property insurance that covers damage to a building while it is under construction, including materials and equipment physically at the project site.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning

questions.q: A standard contract clause requires a vendor to promise to defend the agency, pay legal fees, and cover damages if the agency is sued due to the vendor's negligence. This risk transfer mechanism is known as:
questions.explain: An indemnification or 'hold harmless' clause is a contractual agreement where one party (the vendor) agrees to assume the liability and legal defense costs for damages arising out of their own performance or negligence, transferring risk away from the public agency.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning

questions.q: To ensure that a vendor's Commercial General Liability policy provides direct protection and defense coverage to the public agency in the event of a lawsuit, the procurement officer must require the vendor to list the agency as:
options: An Additional Insured on the Certificate of Insurance (COI).
questions.explain: Being named as an 'Additional Insured' gives the agency status under the vendor's policy, meaning the vendor's insurance company must defend and cover the agency if it is sued as a result of the vendor's operations.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning

questions.q: In the context of Enterprise Risk Management, purchasing an insurance policy or requiring a contractor to provide a performance bond are examples of which risk response strategy?
questions.explain: Risk transfer involves shifting the financial burden and consequences of a risk to a third party. Insurance policies, surety bonds, and indemnification clauses are classic mechanisms for transferring risk away from the agency.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning

questions.q: A hurricane unexpectedly devastates the manufacturing plant of a contracted supplier, rendering them entirely unable to deliver vehicles to the agency. The vendor will likely invoke which contract clause to be excused from liability for the delay?
questions.explain: A Force Majeure (often called 'Act of God') clause excuses a party from fulfilling their contractual obligations when extraordinary, unforeseeable events beyond their control (e.g., natural disasters, wars, pandemics) make performance impossible.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning

questions.q: A risk manager asks the procurement officer to ensure the vendor's insurance includes a 'Waiver of Subrogation' in favor of the agency. What does this mean?
options: The agency waives its right to inspect the vendor's work.
The vendor's insurance company waives its right to sue the public agency to recover funds it paid out for a claim on behalf of the vendor.
The vendor agrees to waive all payments until the project is perfect.
The agency agrees to use a subordinate court for litigation.
questions.explain: Subrogation is an insurer's legal right to pursue a third party that caused an insurance loss to the insured. A Waiver of Subrogation prevents the vendor's insurance company from turning around and suing the public agency to recoup the money they paid out.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning

questions.q: An agency is procuring an online citizen portal where citizens will input credit card information and personal addresses to pay municipal utility bills. What specific insurance policy is an absolute necessity for the portal vendor to maintain?
questions.explain: Whenever a vendor handles, processes, or stores Personally Identifiable Information (PII) or Payment Card Industry (PCI) data, Cyber Liability Insurance is critical. It covers the immense costs associated with data breaches, hack investigations, and citizen notification.
